q: Why are Sigmoid and Tanh activations generally avoided in the deep hidden layers of a feedforward network?
options: They are entirely discontinuous functions
They cause vanishing gradient problems
They force all parameter weights to zero
They lack mathematical derivatives
explain: Sigmoid and Tanh functions saturate at extreme inputs, flattening their derivatives. This causes gradients to shrink exponentially during backpropagation.

q: How does adding a dropout layer during training help prevent overfitting in deep neural networks?
options: It scales down large outlier features
It breaks up co-adaptations between neurons
It locks parameter weights to zero
It forces the network to become linear
explain: By randomly deactivating neurons, dropout forces the network to learn redundant representations rather than relying on brittle, co-adapted node relationships.

q: You change your model regularizer from L2 weight decay to L1 regularization. What direct impact do you expect on the weights?
options: Weights will grow exponentially larger
Unimportant weights become exactly zero
All weights will scale uniformly
Weights will oscillate around zero
explain: L1 regularization uses an absolute value penalty that drives less predictive weights to exactly zero, creating a sparse model matrix.

q: Why does batch normalization stabilize and speed up the training of deep neural networks?
options: It completely eliminates the loss function
It reduces internal covariate shift
It forces all weights to match
It deactivates negative activations
explain: Batch normalization standardizes the inputs to each layer across a batch. This mitigates internal covariate shift, allowing higher learning rates.

q: Which parameters does a batch normalization layer learn and optimize dynamically during training?
options: The batch mean and batch variance
The scale gamma and shift beta
The dropout rate and keep rate
The filter weights and stride steps
explain: While mean and variance are computed statistics, gamma (scale) and beta (shift) are backpropagation-trainable parameters that restore representation power.

q: How do Convolutional Neural Networks achieve parameter sharing across an entire input image?
options: By using identical weights at every layer
By applying the same filter across patches
By keeping latent vector values static
By sharing biases across multiple batches
explain: CNNs use parameter sharing by sweeping the same filter across all spatial regions, allowing them to detect a feature regardless of its location.

q: You want to design an unsupervised system that automatically extracts semantic features without manual engineering. What field is this?
options: Rule-based programming
Representation learning
Tabular classification
Linear regression analysis
explain: Representation learning automatically discovers the underlying variations and structural features needed for tasks directly from raw input data.

q: What core difference separates a generative model from a traditional discriminative model?
options: Generative models only support continuous labels
Generative models model the joint probability
Generative models require labeled target splits
Generative models maximize classification accuracy
explain: Generative models learn the joint probability distribution P(x, y) to capture data traits, while discriminative models learn conditional probability P(y|x) for boundaries.

q: Why does a Variational Autoencoder include a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence term in its loss function?
options: To maximize structural reconstruction error
To force the latent distribution toward a prior
To eliminate the encoder network completely
To scale parameter weights to zero
explain: The KL divergence term forces the learned latent distribution to match a standard Gaussian prior, ensuring a continuous, smoothly samplable latent space.

q: Your GAN generator keeps producing the exact same realistic output image regardless of the random input noise vector. What issue is this?
options: Vanishing gradients
Mode collapse
Internal covariate shift
Overfitting under-recovery
explain: Mode collapse occurs when the generator finds a single output that consistently fools the discriminator, causing it to stop generating diverse samples.

q: Why do traditional Recurrent Neural Networks struggle to maintain long-term dependencies across text paragraphs?
options: They lack recurrent connection weights
Gradients vanish or explode over time
They cannot process character strings
They scale sequence lengths to zero
explain: Because RNNs repeatedly multiply gradients across time steps, the backpropagated signal vanishes or explodes when dealing with long context sequences.

q: How do LSTMs successfully preserve historical data across hundreds of steps without vanishing gradients?
options: By removing activation layers entirely
By using a linear cell state with gates
By resetting parameters at each sequence
By processing words in parallel matrices
explain: LSTMs use a continuous linear cell state regulated by forget, input, and output gates, allowing long-term historical gradients to flow unimpeded.

q: What is the primary architectural advantage of a Transformer network over a Recurrent Neural Network?
options: Transformers process sequences in a loop
Transformers process entire sequences in parallel
Transformers use fewer parameter layers
Transformers require zero activation functions
explain: Transformers replace loops with self-attention, processing whole sequences in parallel. This significantly accelerates hardware acceleration and training speed.

q: Why do Diffusion Models generally produce more stable synthesis results than Generative Adversarial Networks?
options: They use a simple linear classification loss
They train via stable iterative step objectives
They eliminate the neural network encoder
They ignore noise distribution parameters
explain: GANs rely on a volatile minimax game that is prone to instability. Diffusion models train on a stable mean-squared error objective to reverse incremental noise.

q: You are building a model to handle audio waveforms and text tokens simultaneously. How does a multimodal network merge these streams?
options: By converting text into raw wave audio
By projecting embeddings into a shared space
By removing attention heads from text
By using separate linear classification heads
explain: Multimodal models project different inputs into a shared geometric embedding space, allowing the network to compute attention across text and audio features.

q: How does an LSTM forget gate determine what historical information to discard from the running cell state?
options: By setting all positive weights to zero
By passing inputs through a sigmoid layer
By flattening the sequence across channels
By subtracting validation loss statistics
explain: The forget gate applies a sigmoid function to output values between 0 (discard completely) and 1 (keep entirely) for the cell state components.

q: Your network validation loss drops during training, but your training outputs show highly unstable, fluctuating updates. What issue are you spotting?
options: Vanishing structural dependencies
Exploding gradients in backpropagation
A learning rate that is too low
Mode collapse inside the autoencoder
explain: Exploding gradients cause massive parameter updates, making weights jump erratically. This manifests as highly volatile training loss curves.

q: Why does a diffusion model perform better than an auto-regressive model when synthesizing highly detailed large image matrices?
options: It scales context length exponentially
It generates images via non-causal parallel steps
It eliminates the need for any decoder
It operates exclusively on low-dimension text
explain: Auto-regressive models must generate images pixel-by-pixel, which is slow and memory-intensive. Diffusion models generate all pixels in parallel over denoising steps.

q: You notice your model's early convolutional filters are extracting identical primitive edge features across two different tasks. What justifies this trait?
options: The network has reached structural saturation
Low-level visual representations generalize widely
The optimizer is trapped in a local minimum
The dropout rate is scaling parameters
explain: Early layers in computer vision extract generic feature primitives like edges and textures. This makes them highly reusable across different tasks via transfer learning.

q: Your autoencoder reconstructs clean images perfectly, but selecting random points from the latent space yields nonsense shapes. What is missing?
options: A larger convolutional filter grid
Probabilistic structure on the latent space
Additional fully connected layer blocks
A higher learning rate configuration
explain: Standard autoencoders leave gaps in the latent space. Variational Autoencoders solve this by enforcing a continuous, probabilistic Gaussian distribution.

q: What happens mathematically when you configure a convolutional stride length equal to the filter width size?
options: The receptive fields overlap by half
The adjacent receptive fields do not overlap
The output dimension expands exponentially
The boundary padding blocks are skipped
explain: When the stride equals the filter width, the window moves exactly to the edge of the previous patch, processing adjacent sections without overlap.

q: How does a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) structurally simplify the multi-gate processing framework found in standard LSTMs?
options: It completely removes the hidden state layer
It combines cell and hidden states into one
It utilizes parallel self-attention matrices
It completely avoids backpropagation steps
explain: GRUs combine the cell state and hidden state, using only update and reset gates. This simplifies the architecture and speeds up computation.

q: Why does a self-attention mechanism scale its calculation complexity quadratically relative to the input sequence length?
options: It maps tokens to multiple spatial channels
Every token computes a score against every other token
It requires a loop across multiple layers
It expands feature vector size per step
explain: Self-attention creates an N x N matrix where every token matches against every other token in the sequence, making its complexity $O(N^2)$.

q: You want your network output to match continuous targets while penalizing large errors heavily without dropping smaller noise. Which loss fits?
options: Categorical cross-entropy validation loss
Mean Squared Error loss
Softmax distribution cross-entropy
Binary classification step functions
explain: Mean Squared Error squares residuals, penalizing large discrepancies heavily. This makes it ideal for standard continuous regression tasks.

q: Your deep network updates parameter values successfully in late layers, but early layer weight metrics remain completely static. What is happening?
options: Exploding gradients inside layers
Vanishing gradients during backpropagation
Optimal parameter convergence states
Asymmetric weight distribution traps
explain: As gradients travel backward through many layers, repeated multiplication can cause them to shrink to near zero. This leaves early layer weights unadjusted.
